titulo: Spain is four languages and one very old argument
subtitulo: You don't need to speak Catalan, Basque or Galician — you need to recognise them, and to know which subject to leave alone
_cenaProposta: Second glass of wine on a terrace, and the older man at the next table turns round and asks you straight out what the British think about Catalan independence.
_cenaBloqueadaPor: G4: narração com 931 chars/clipe (teto 120) e 8 de 8 clipes acima de 320. Insanável sem repartir a narração, o que obriga a regravar. Decisão do dono.
frasePiso: You will hand a political question straight back without picking a side, and you will know the five subjects not to open with somebody you met twenty minutes ago. Most visitors spend a fortnight in Spain without ever noticing there was anything there to get right.
permissao: You will not offend anybody by speaking Spanish in Barcelona. Not a soul. Bon dia is a courtesy, never a requirement, and courtesy is free. And you are allowed to have no view at all on the argument: «no conozco bien el tema» is a complete and honest answer, not a dodge. There is no legal risk here either — this is argued out loud on national television every week of the year.
espelho: Saying you like both Barça and Madrid is the bit that reads as odd there. At home splitting the difference is good manners; at that table it reads as not having listened, and it is the one answer worse than picking a side.

fichasCulturais.sinal: Second glass of wine, and the man at the next table turns round and asks you straight out what the British make of Catalan independence.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: He is picking a fight, or testing me, and whatever I say next is going to be the wrong answer.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The subject is argued openly on national television every week of the year, so putting it to a foreigner is closer to handing you the interesting topic than to setting a trap. What he wants is the floor, not your verdict.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Hand it back — «no conozco bien el tema, cuénteme» — and then ask and listen instead of ruling.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the half hour of the evening where somebody explains their own country to you, which is the part a visitor almost never gets offered.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not when you are the one who opened it. The same subject raised by you, twenty minutes after meeting someone, reads as the opposite — and that is the one place the escape line does not rescue you, because you started it.

fichasCulturais.sinal: Someone at the counter switches to Catalan with the barman, and you catch yourself deciding what they must think about independence.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: They speak the language, so they want out — that is what speaking it is for.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The two do not track. Catalan-speaking Catalans have polled majority-against independence in measurement after measurement, and people notice being read off a map they never drew.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Ask where they sit instead of working it out from the language, the accent or the city.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: The conversation goes somewhere you could not have guessed, and you leave with a person’s version instead of a headline’s.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not as a rule about staying vague. Once they have told you where they stand, carrying on as though it were still open reads as not having listened either.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You are called guiri inside your first three days, usually by somebody who is smiling while they say it.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I have just been insulted, and everybody at the table watched it happen.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: It is the ordinary word for a visitor from northern Europe, and it runs from neutral to affectionate far more often than it runs the other way. It describes what you look like, not what you are worth.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Take it as said. Smile and carry on — asking whether it was meant badly is what turns a light word into a heavy one.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get to be the visitor who is comfortable being one, and the table relaxes at the same speed you do.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not in a residential street at eleven in the morning in swim shorts, a bumbag and socks with sandals. There the word is being used accurately — and in Barcelona the missing shirt is also a hundred-and-twenty to three-hundred-euro question, taken on the spot, by card. fatosDatados.fonte: docs/pesquisa-espanha.md §7.7(a) e a tabela de ordenança — FATO, ordenança de civismo de Barcelona aprovada dez/2025, em vigor fev/2026: €120–300, cobrada no ato, por cartão. ⚠️ DIVERGÊNCIA MEDIDA (1): o áudio c03b-20 diz «a hundred-and-twenty-euro fine», que é o piso da faixa e não a faixa. ⚠️ DIVERGÊNCIA MEDIDA (2), corrigida neste campo por revisor: o áudio c03b-20 diz «as you learned in 3A» e a versão anterior desta fonte repetia «Recitado de A03/3A, onde a multa é ensinada» — as duas estão erradas. A03 é ep-a03.json («Who they think they are», ordem 31) e não menciona a multa em nenhum clipe; 3A é ep-c03a.json, que tem dissolveEm:[I09,I04,A07] e vai ser apagado, levando junto o clipe c03a-04, o único dele que ensinava a multa. Quem ensina a multa no corpus vigente é I09 (ordem 27, clipe i09-g02), e lá ela sai correta: «a hundred and twenty to three hundred euros, under the civility ordinance in force there since February». Ou seja: a referência cruzada gravada em c03b-20 aponta para uma parte que não vai existir, e o número certo já foi dado ao aluno cinco slots antes. Insanável sem regravar; entra na mesma decisão do dono que o `_cenaBloqueadaPor`.

steps.pt: Part 3B, and let's start with the fact most visitors arrive without: Spain has four languages. Castilian Spanish — the one you're learning — is official everywhere, and it is the language you will be answered in the moment anyone hears your accent. Alongside it, Catalan is co-official in Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearics; Basque in the Basque Country and part of Navarre; Galician in Galicia. Roughly speaking, that's about two in every five Spaniards living somewhere with a second official language. Now the permission, and it's a big one, so I'll say it before anything else: you will not offend anybody by speaking Spanish in Barcelona. Not a soul. Bon dia is a courtesy, never a requirement, and courtesy is free. What you do need is to recognise the other three when they turn up on a door, a menu or a departure board — because they will. Warm-up as usual while I talk: one tap per syllable, all the same size, palm flat and still on the vowels.

steps.promptPt: Callback from 3A first. A square in Valencia, a can in your hand, no sign in sight. Stop someone and ask whether it's allowed. Speak now.
steps.pt: Excuse me — is drinking allowed here?

Catalan first, because that's where most of you are going. Catalan is not a dialect of Spanish, it is not an accent, and it is not Spanish spoken badly. It's a separate Romance language with its own grammar, its own spelling and about a thousand years of literature, and calling it a dialect is the single fastest way to annoy someone who has been perfectly friendly to you all evening. That's the consequence half of this: here's the action half, and it takes two seconds. Say bon dia when you walk into a bar in Barcelona or Girona, and watch what happens to the service. It's not that they need it — they'll switch to Spanish for you immediately. It's that you bothered. Three more and you're done for life: si us plau, please; moltes gràcies, thank you very much; and adéu on the way out, because in Spain you greet on the way in and on the way out, and in Catalonia you can do both in Catalan.
Good morning / hello. — Catalan. Say it on the way in.
Thank you very much. — Catalan. Note the ending is a soft 'uh', not the Spanish 'ah'.

steps.promptPt: You push open the door of a small neighbourhood bar in Gràcia. Four locals at the counter look up. Greet the room — in Catalan. Speak now.
steps.pt: Good morning / hello.
Bye. — Catalan. Two syllables, both fully paid.

steps.promptPt: You've paid, you've got your coat, you're leaving the same bar. Don't just walk out — say goodbye in Catalan. Speak now.
steps.pt: Bye. — Catalan. Two syllables, both fully paid.

Two words each for the other two, and then I'll stop, because this genuinely isn't a language course. Basque — euskara — is the strange one, and it's worth knowing why: it is not related to Spanish, or to French, or to Latin, or to anything else alive. Nobody knows where it came from. Say kaixo for hello, which is easier than it looks — 'kai-sho' — and eskerrik asko for thank you. In Galicia, which sounds far more Portuguese than you're expecting, it's bo día in the morning and grazas for thanks. That's it. Four words. Nobody expects a single one of them from you, which is exactly why they land.
Thank you. — Basque. Nothing in it will remind you of Spanish, and that's the point.
Thanks. — Galician. Same 'th' as gracias, one syllable shorter.

Now the part that actually matters day to day, and it's pure recognition — nothing to produce here, just ears and eyes. In a neighbourhood bar in Barcelona, Girona, Valencia, Palma, Bilbao or Santiago, the menu on the wall and the sign on the door may be in the co-official language only. Not to make a point at you; because that's the language of the street they're on. So: three sets, listen and file them. Floor of success, and it's a low one — if the only thing you ever manage is spotting sortida on an exit and tancat on a door, you have not wasted this section, because those two are the ones that leave you standing outside a closed shop or walking past your own exit.
👂 Catalan signs: EXIT · OPEN · CLOSED. Sortida is the Catalan salida; tancat is cerrado.
👂 Catalan doors: PULL · PUSH · TOILETS. Careful — estirar here is PULL, and it looks nothing like the Spanish tirar you learned.
👂 Basque: EXIT · TOILET. Galician: EXIT · CLOSED. Four words, and they're the four you'd hate to miss.

George again, on the argument. And here the good news comes first, because it's the opposite of what you might expect from a course that keeps warning you about things: there is no legal risk whatsoever in this. None. Spain is a settled democracy, opinions about Catalonia are argued loudly on national television every week of the year, and nobody is going to arrest a tourist for having a view. The risk is entirely social — you can ruin an evening, and your relationship with the person serving you, in about nine seconds. So: don't raise Catalan independence, ETA and the Basque Country, Franco, the monarchy or the Civil War with somebody you met twenty minutes ago. It is the exact equivalent of walking into a pub in Belfast and asking which side the family was on. If they raise it — and they might, because it's genuinely interesting to them — listen and ask, don't rule. Never guess which side someone is on from their city, their accent or the language they speak: Catalan-speaking Catalans have come out majority against independence in poll after poll, so the mental map of 'speaks Catalan, wants out' is simply wrong, and the person can tell you're using it. Don't talk about Spain and Catalonia as two countries, and don't do the other one either — 'it's all just Spain really, isn't it' — because those two sentences offend opposite halves of the room. And football is politics conducted by other means: Barça and Madrid is not small talk, and saying you support both is the only answer worse than picking one. Here is your escape hatch, and it works because it's true.

steps.es: No conozco bien el tema, cuénteme.
steps.pinyin: noh koh-NOHTH-koh byen el TEH-mah, KWEN-teh-meh
steps.pt: I don't really know the subject — tell me about it.
steps.tts: No conozco bien el tema, cuénteme.

steps.promptPt: Second glass of wine, and the older man at the next table turns round and asks you straight out what the British think about Catalan independence. Don't have an opinion — hand him the floor. Speak now.
steps.es: No conozco bien el tema, cuénteme.
steps.pinyin: noh koh-NOHTH-koh byen el TEH-mah, KWEN-teh-meh
steps.pt: I don't really know the subject — tell me about it.

One more thing, and then a promise. In July twenty twenty-four, protesters in Barcelona sprayed tourists sitting on terraces with water pistols, and in June twenty twenty-five there were coordinated demonstrations in Barcelona, Palma, Lisbon, Venice and Naples. You may have seen the photographs, and you may have arrived slightly nervous. So, accurately: the anger is about housing. Barcelona's housing costs have risen around sixty-eight per cent in a decade, that is the stated root of it, and it is aimed at the model, not at the person carrying the suitcase. 'Barcelona hates tourists' is false and paranoid and I'd rather you didn't repeat it. What is true is that exactly two behaviours put you on the wrong side of it instantly, and both are free to avoid: wheeling a suitcase down a residential street at two in the morning, and being loud on the stairwell. That's it. That's the whole ask. And finally — guiri. You will be called it, probably within your first three days. It's slang for a northern European tourist, usually with no hostility in it and sometimes with real affection, and it is not a slur. Although. If you are standing in a residential street at eleven in the morning in swim shorts, a bumbag and socks with sandals, then you have earned the word fairly — and, as you learned in 3A, you may also have earned yourself a hundred-and-twenty-euro fine for the missing shirt.
Good morning / hello. — Catalan.

steps.es: No conozco bien el tema, cuénteme.
steps.pinyin: noh koh-NOHTH-koh byen el TEH-mah, KWEN-teh-meh
steps.pt: I don't really know the subject — tell me about it.

In focus, briefly. That escape line you just practised has a switch in it worth knowing. Cuénteme is the usted version — the polite one, for the older gentleman at the next table, for anyone in a uniform, for a formal counter. With someone your own age in a bar it's cuéntame, with an 'a', and that's the version you'll use more often, because in Spain tú is the default and usted is the exception, not the other way round. Same sentence, one vowel, completely different social temperature. And one line on why any of this exists, for your own map: Catalan, Basque and Galician were suppressed under Franco and were only restored to official status with the constitution of nineteen seventy-eight. When someone tells you the language on their menu is a political act, they are not being dramatic — for their grandparents it literally was. You don't have to have a view about that. You just have to know it's the water everyone's swimming in.

That's part 3B, and that's the Culture track finished. You can greet a room in Catalan, thank someone in Basque and Galician, read an exit sign in three languages you don't speak, and — most useful of all — you can hand back a political question without dropping it. Bon dia going in, adéu going out, and if the argument comes to you: no conozco bien el tema, cuénteme. Adéu, and enjoy Spain.

aprofundar.titulo: Four languages, one argument — the detail (optional)

secoes.corpo: Castilian Spanish is official across the whole territory and is what this course teaches. Catalan is co-official in Catalonia, the Balearics and the Valencian Community (where it is officially called valencià); Basque (euskara) in the Basque Country and northern Navarre; Galician (galego) in Galicia. Catalan and Galician are Romance languages — you will half-recognise a lot of written Catalan and most written Galician. Basque is unrelated to any known living language, which is why nothing in it looks familiar. You will be served in Spanish everywhere; the co-official language matters to you almost entirely in writing.

exemplos.es: Kaixo · Eskerrik asko / Bo día · Grazas
exemplos.pt: Basque: hello · thank you / Galician: good morning · thanks

secoes.corpo: Catalan: obert / tancat (open / closed) · sortida (exit) · entrada · lavabos or serveis (toilets) · estirar / empènyer (pull / push — note that estirar is PULL, which trips up anyone who has just learned Spanish tirar) · esmorzar / dinar / sopar (breakfast / lunch / dinner, and useful for reading opening hours) · preu (price) · pa (bread) · aigua (water). Basque: irteera (exit) · komuna (toilet) · itxita (closed). Galician: saída (exit) · aberto / pechado (open / closed). Nothing here is ever produced out loud — it goes in your eyes, not your mouth.

secoes.titulo: The political topic: no legal risk, all social risk
secoes.corpo: Unlike some destinations, there is no legal exposure here at all — Spain debates Catalonia, the monarchy and the Civil War openly and constantly. What you can lose is the evening. Don't open the subject with strangers. If it opens on you, ask and listen: 'No conozco bien el tema, cuénteme' (usted) or 'cuéntame' (tú) hands the floor back and almost always ends the pressure. Never infer someone's position from their city, accent or language — Catalan-speaking Catalans have polled majority-against independence in multiple measurements. Avoid both 'Spain and Catalonia' as separate countries and 'it's all just Spain', which offend opposite sides. Football is not neutral ground; claiming to support both Barça and Madrid is worse than picking one.

secoes.corpo: In July 2024 protesters in Barcelona sprayed water pistols at tourists on terraces; in June 2025 coordinated protests took place in Barcelona, Palma, Lisbon, Venice and Naples under the SET network, with 'tourist go home' stickers on hotel doors. The declared root is housing: local authorities have cited a rise of about 68% in Barcelona housing costs over the decade. It targets the model, not the individual. Two behaviours put a visitor on the wrong side of it instantly and both are free to avoid: wheeling a suitcase through a residential street at 2am, and noise on a shared stairwell. 'Guiri' is slang for a northern European tourist and is normally affectionate or neutral, not a slur.
